title: Latency Sampling Notebook — staged trace breakdowns (p50/p95/p99)
content:
Purpose:
This notebook collects sampled end-to-end traces (p50/p95/p99) across recent production and dedicated deployments to identify dominant latency contributors and plausible mitigations. Focus: per-stage breakdowns for short/med/long contexts and comparisons with/without KV cache hits and with different batching regimes.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- p50 is dominated by model execution for long sequences but by edge+stream chunking overhead for short responses.
- p95/p99 show large tail contributions from two sources: worker queue wait (spikes under bursty arrival) and periodic kernel stalls (observed on a100 nodes at 10–30% load).
- KV cache hits reduce model-exec tail substantially for multi-turns (p99 down ~450ms on 512-context), but introduce sporadic metadata lookup spikes when cache sharding crosses worker boundaries.
- Batching reduces per-token cost but increases p95 by ~120–200ms under low-concurrency flows; safe to use on Dedicated but avoid for low-latency-hosted routes.

Methodology:
- Sampling: 1% random sampling of production requests across US west region; supplementary 100% trace capture for specific smoke windows on dedicated pools.
- Time window: 2025-02-01 to 2025-02-14 for baseline; focused investigations 2025-02-20 to 2025-02-28.
- Models: redwood-4b-8k-quant (default hosted), redwood-14b-v2 (dedicated), community-7b-qat (burst test).
- Sequence length buckets: short (<=32 tokens), medium (33–256), long (257–2048).
- Stages captured in traces (order preserved): ingress-edge, auth-rate-limit, router, worker-queue-wait, worker-init, tokenizer-encode, kv-cache-lookup, model-exec-first-token, model-exec-subsequent, kernel-kernel-stall, output-format, network-stream-chunks, client-ack.
- Aggregation: compute p50/p95/p99 per-stage and sum to derive end-to-end percentiles; compare "sum of percentile stages" vs "trace-level percentiles" to ensure no major aggregation bias.

Selected aggregated numbers (representative slices):
1) Hosted (redwood-4b-8k-quant), short responses (<=32), no KV cache:
- end-to-end: p50=78ms, p95=220ms, p99=410ms
- per-stage (p95): ingress-edge=18ms, router=10ms, worker-queue-wait=55ms, tokenizer-encode=8ms, model-exec-first-token=70ms, output-format=20ms, stream-chunking=35ms
- note: p99 shows a long tail from worker-queue-wait (200–600ms in individual traces) when burst arrives.

2) Dedicated (redwood-14b-v2), medium responses (33–256), KV hit vs miss:
- KV hit (cache hit on local worker): end-to-end p50=190ms, p95=430ms, p99=820ms
  - model-exec-subsequent tokens dominate: p95=260ms, kernel-stalls contribute ~80–140ms in p99 cases
- KV miss (fallback to full model run): end-to-end p50=480ms, p95=980ms, p99=1,740ms
  - model-exec-first-token balloons (p95 ~600–900ms) due to full KV load and longer kernel cold paths.

3) Dedicated, long responses (>=512), mixed batching 4–16: 
- batching 4: end-to-end p50=620ms, p95=1,120ms, p99=1,900ms
- batching 16: end-to-end p50=580ms (slightly better throughput), p95=1,460ms (noticeable tail regression), p99=2,400ms
- interpretation: batching helps average latency under stable high concurrency but worsens tail when arrival is bursty and queue wait times spike.

Representative trace excerpts (samples) — timestamps are relative elapsed ms from request receive:
- trace_id: trc-20250222-01
  stages: ingress-edge=12, router=6, worker-queue-wait=18, worker-init=3, tokenizer-encode=7, kv-cache-lookup=2, model-exec-first-token=82, model-exec-subsequent=[24,22,20,...], output-format=14, stream-chunking=9, total=197ms

- trace_id: trc-20250224-11 (p99 example)
  stages: ingress-edge=14, router=7, worker-queue-wait=480, worker-init=4, tokenizer-encode=9, kv-cache-lookup=12 (cross-shard hop), model-exec-first-token=610 (kernel stall observed), kernel-kernel-stall=210, output-format=26, total=1,572ms

Observations / Hypotheses:
1) Worker queue wait is the highest variance contributor to p95/p99 under bursty arrival. Hypothesis: current autoscaling and request routing thresholding permits short-lived request pileups before new workers come online.
2) Kernel stalls on some A100 nodes correlate with certain CUDA/driver versions and occasional memory fragmentation. Hypothesis: periodic defragmentation/worker recycling reduces tail.
3) KV cache sharding/hot keys: KV cache local hits are fast; cross-worker lookups introduce spikes in kv-cache-lookup stage due to RPC hops. Hypothesis: improve affinity/routing or replicate hot prefixes.
4) Streaming chunkization (server-side chunking for streaming tokens) adds constant overhead on short responses and can drive p50 for very short completions.

Quick checks already run:
- Turned off batching on a sample hosted route for 48h — observed p95 drop for short responses but throughput and cost increased ~12%.
- Deployed worker-restart experiment on a dedicated pool (weekly stagger) — p99 reduced by ~10% during maintenance windows but insufficient for full tail.
- Captured kernel metrics and driver versions — correlated 6 cases of p99 spikes with driver 525.x on a100-1.

Actionable next steps (practical experiments):
- INF-3421 (priority): implement "fast-path" routing that detects low-token responses and pins them to low-latency workers (no batching, higher pre-warmed pool). Measure p95/p99 improvement and cost delta.
- Experiment: increase sampling rate in surge hours to 5% to catch more rare tail modes; add span-level tags for driver/kernel version to traces.
- Short-term mitigation: reinforce autoscaler aggressiveness for worker provisioning with a "burst cushion" (small warm pool) for hosted API routes.
- KV mitigation: evaluate replicating hot prefixes to avoid cross-worker RPCs; prototype sticky routing for multi-turn sessions (session affinity).
- Kernel investigation: run controlled repros on affected A100s with driver 525.x, test later driver 530.x; add periodic memory compact step during low-traffic windows.

Open questions / notes for follow-up:
- What percent of p99 is caused by network jitter vs local worker stalls? We need additional network-level spans between edge and worker.
- Is there a measurable user-visible improvement if we drop server-streaming chunk size from 128 tokens to 64 for short routes? (A/B test candidate).
- How much cost increase if we maintain a 5% warm buffer of pre-warmed workers for hosted-high-priority routes?

Planned experiments and owners:
- Fast-path low-latency workers: owner Ravi Patel, target prototype in 2 sprints, metric: hosted p95 for <=32 tokens route. (JIRA-INF-3470)
- KV prefix replication proof-of-concept: owner Lin Chen, target 3 weeks, metric: reduction in kv-cache-lookup p99 frequency.
- Kernel-driver repro: owner Jordan Kim, target 1 week to produce deterministic repro and driver test matrix.

Appendix: useful commands / quick trace queries
- pull traces for trace_id prefix: go-trace-cli --since 2025-02-20 --trace-prefix trc-20250224 --output json
- histogram by stage: internal-telemetryql 'histogram(stage.duration_ms) by stage where env=prod and model=redwood-14b-v2'
- quick slack thread: see #serving-runtime (thread ts: 1700000000.000100)

Notes to self: keep a running list of "p99 fingerprints" (kernel-stall, queue-pileup, kv-cross-shard) and capture at least 20 examples per fingerprint to make targeted fixes. This doc will evolve into a short-living runbook for triaging latency spikes.

End of notebook.
